rationale:
The tests adequately cover `requirements.sdk.graph.search.StructuralRule`. Each obligation maps to a test that exercises it and asserts the outcome.

- **`languages` lists the accepted grammar names.**
  - `crates/trust-but-verify/src/structural.rs#mod[tests]/fn[rules_compile_for_every_grammar_and_report_invalid_input]` compiles a rule for rust, python, typescript, tsx, css, markdown, toml and yaml.
  - It asserts `tested == StructuralRule::languages()`, so the list is complete and in the same order.
  - `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/search.rs#fn[compile_once_and_search_supplied_source]` also checks that `languages()` contains `rust`.
- **Compilation reports an unknown language or an invalid rule core, with no source to search.**
  - The first test above checks `cobol` and `plain-text` for the error "unknown structural search language".
  - It checks a missing `rule` key, an unexpected `fix` key, an unknown kind, and a bogus rule key, each for the expected message.
  - `fn[compile_once_and_search_supplied_source]` asserts `SourceError::Invalid` for `plain-text` and for an empty core.
- **`extensions` has at least one entry and no leading dots.**
  - The per-grammar test asserts `!rule.extensions().is_empty()` for every language.
  - `fn[compile_once_and_search_supplied_source]` asserts that the rust extensions contain `"rs"`.
  - I found no assertion that the extensions of the other languages lack leading dots. `extensions()` in `sources/public.rs` returns the static `Profile` data unchanged, and the profile tables I read list bare names such as `py`, `ts` and `yml`. It has no conditional or transformation of its own, so I treat this as an acceptable exemption rather than a gap.
- **`matches` returns distinct, byte-offset half-open spans ordered by start, then end.**
  - `fn[compile_once_and_search_supplied_source]` covers nested matches ordered by start (`f(g())`, `g()`, `h()`).
  - It covers same-start matches ordered by end (`f()`, `f()()`).
  - It includes a multi-byte `é`, sliced with `&text[span]`, so the offsets are byte offsets.
  - It covers empty input returning no matches.
  - It runs the same compiled rule against several texts, which shows offsets refer to the input of each call.
  - `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/search.rs#fn[nodes_covering_the_same_source_produce_one_span]` shows that `source_file` and `function_item` nodes covering the same bytes give exactly one span, with each kind alone and with both together. This covers the distinctness requirement.
  - The per-grammar test also checks the matched text for every grammar.
- **`SourceProject::search_structure` uses the same matcher.** `crates/trust-but-verify/src/agent/project_sources.rs#mod[tests]/fn[structural_tags_select_only_the_original_enclosing_item]` asserts that `rule.matches(file text)` equals the spans of the `search_structure` hits.

I found no unacknowledged gap, and no acknowledgments apply.

text: A `sources::StructuralRule` is a structural query compiled for repeated searches
of text supplied by the caller. `languages` lists the bundled grammar names
accepted by `compile`. Compilation reports an unknown language or an invalid
ast-grep rule core, even when there is no source to search. `extensions` lists
the language's filename extensions without leading dots and contains at least one entry.
`matches` searches the supplied UTF-8 text and returns distinct half-open byte
spans ordered by start, then end. Offsets refer to that input on each call.
`SourceProject::search_structure` uses the same matcher for project files.
